subtopic_detail: Abrupt severe hypertension with rising creatinine, fragmented red cells and a bland urinary sediment weeks after starting moderate dose corticosteroid for early diffuse skin thickening
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44 year old woman admitted with a three day headache and blurred vision. Her hands and forearms have become tight and thickened over the past eight months and she has had cold painful colour changes in her fingers for a year.

Her rheumatologist started prednisolone 20 mg daily five weeks ago for troublesome joint pain. She has no fever, no rash and no recent diarrhoea. Her blood pressure was 126/78 mmHg at her clinic visit two months ago and is now 214/122 mmHg. Her creatinine has risen from 68 to 212 micromol/L over three weeks. The blood film shows fragmented red cells and her platelet count has fallen, while her urinalysis shows no casts and only a trace of protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 214/122 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Skin thickening over the fingers, hands and forearms extending above the elbows, digital pitting scars, bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy, no rash, no synovitis, chest clear, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 212 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 68 three weeks ago, haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-155), platelets 84 x10^9/L (150-450), blood film with fragmented red cells, lactate dehydrogenase 620 units per litre (120-250), urinalysis with trace protein and no red cell casts, ADAMTS13 activity 62 per cent, antinuclear antibody positive with a nucleolar pattern

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Start an intravenous labetalol infusion and titrate against the blood pressure response
options.rationale: Beta blockade lowers the pressure without addressing the renin driven mechanism and may worsen the digital vasospasm, and controlling the number by another route does not protect the kidney. The near pair is that both lower blood pressure but only one alters the disease process. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

options.text: Start oral captopril and increase the dose rapidly against the blood pressure response
options.rationale: Abrupt severe hypertension with a rising creatinine and a microangiopathic blood picture in early diffuse skin disease, particularly after corticosteroid exposure, is treated with a short acting angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor titrated aggressively, and this is the intervention that changed the outcome of the condition from almost uniformly fatal. A rising creatinine after starting it is expected and is not a reason to stop. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and increase her maintenance prednisolone
options.rationale: Corticosteroid at doses of 15 mg daily or more is a recognised precipitant of this complication rather than a treatment for it, and escalating the dose compounds the problem. The steroid should be reduced as fast as her other disease allows. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

options.text: Start daily plasma exchange and give intravenous methylprednisolone alongside it
options.rationale: Plasma exchange treats thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which is suggested by fragmented cells and thrombocytopenia but requires severely deficient ADAMTS13 activity below 10 per cent. Her activity of 62 per cent excludes it, which is the finding that redirects the whole assessment. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic microangiopathy)

options.text: Start intravenous cyclophosphamide and arrange urgent percutaneous renal biopsy
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is used for progressive interstitial lung disease in this condition and has no role in the renal complication, and biopsy in the setting of severe hypertension and thrombocytopenia carries substantial bleeding risk. The diagnosis is clinical and treatment must not wait for tissue. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

explanation.summary: Renal crisis complicates diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis in around one in ten patients and clusters in the first four to five years of disease, when the skin changes are progressing most rapidly. The classical picture is the abrupt onset of accelerated hypertension with an acute rise in creatinine, often accompanied by a microangiopathic anaemia with thrombocytopenia, headache, visual disturbance and sometimes seizures or pulmonary oedema. The urinary sediment is characteristically bland, which separates it from a glomerulonephritis, and the microangiopathy leads many to consider thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura until ADAMTS13 activity comes back normal. Corticosteroid exposure at 15 mg of prednisolone daily or more is the best established precipitant, which is why steroids are used sparingly and at the lowest effective dose in early diffuse disease. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibition, titrated rapidly regardless of an initial rise in creatinine, transformed the prognosis, though a proportion still require dialysis, and recovery of renal function can occur over many months.
key_points: Risk is highest in early diffuse skin disease within the first five years
Prednisolone at 15 mg daily or more is the best established precipitant
A bland urinary sediment separates this from glomerulonephritis
Normal ADAMTS13 activity excludes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Continue the inhibitor despite an early rise in creatinine
explanation.pearls: Patients with early diffuse disease should be taught to check their blood pressure at home two or three times a week, because the hypertension precedes symptoms and a reading above 150/90 in this group is an indication to present the same day rather than to wait for the next clinic.

subtopic_detail: Uniform swelling of an entire toe with asymmetric large joint involvement, nail pitting and negative rheumatoid serology after six weeks of an anti-inflammatory drug
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar seeing a 38 year old man referred with four months of joint pain. His left second toe is swollen along its whole length rather than at one joint, his right knee has been swollen for six weeks, and the terminal joints of two fingers on his left hand are painful and swollen.

He has an hour of stiffness in the morning. He has had scaly patches behind both ears for years that he treats with a cream from the pharmacy, and his nails have small pits and lifting at the free edge. He has taken naproxen twice daily for six weeks with only partial relief and continues to miss work as a carpenter. He has no back pain and no eye symptoms, and he has had no diarrhoea or urethral discharge.

data_table.Examination: Uniform swelling of the entire left second toe, swollen right knee with an effusion, synovitis of two distal interphalangeal joints on the left hand, nail pitting and onycholysis of four fingernails, scaly erythematous plaques behind both ears and at the umbilicus, no sacroiliac tenderness, no conjunctival injection
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/h (less than 20), C reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, urate 0.32 mmol/L (0.20-0.45), radiographs of the hands and feet with soft tissue swelling and no erosion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue the anti-inflammatory drug at a higher dose and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Anti-inflammatory drugs relieve symptoms but do not alter progression, and six weeks of an adequate dose with continuing synovitis and time off work has already defined the failure. Escalating the dose buys nothing while joint damage accrues. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor as the first disease modifying treatment
options.rationale: Biological therapy is highly effective and is the right answer for predominant axial disease or for failure of conventional agents, and Australian subsidy requires a documented trial of conventional therapy first. The near pair is that both are disease modifying, but only one is the entry point here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis)

options.text: Start weekly methotrexate with folic acid and review his response in eight weeks
options.rationale: Persistent peripheral synovitis with whole digit swelling and skin and nail disease that has failed six weeks of an anti-inflammatory drug requires a disease modifying agent, and methotrexate is the usual Australian first choice because it treats both the joints and the skin. Early treatment prevents the erosive damage that has not yet appeared on his films. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis)

options.text: Start allopurinol after checking his renal function and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy treats crystal arthritis, which presents with recurrent acute attacks resolving between episodes rather than persistent swelling of an entire digit, and his urate is mid range. Chronic synovitis with nail and skin changes is a different process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Inject the swollen knee with corticosteroid and review his joint symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Intra-articular injection is a useful adjunct for a dominant single joint and will help the knee, but it leaves the toe, the finger joints and the skin untreated. Systemic disease needs systemic treatment. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis)

explanation.summary: Inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis affects up to a third of people with the skin disease and often presents before the skin is recognised, particularly when the plaques are hidden behind the ears, at the umbilicus, in the natal cleft or on the scalp. Its distinguishing features are asymmetry, involvement of the terminal finger joints, uniform swelling of an entire digit from combined joint and tendon sheath inflammation, inflammation at tendon insertions, nail pitting and onycholysis, and negative rheumatoid serology. Presentations range from an oligoarticular peripheral pattern through a symmetrical polyarthritis to predominantly spinal disease, and each pattern drives a different treatment choice. Conventional agents including methotrexate, leflunomide and sulfasalazine are used for peripheral disease, while axial disease responds poorly to them and moves directly to biological therapy. Screening for the arthritis in every patient with psoriasis matters because delay of even six months is associated with worse radiographic and functional outcomes.
key_points: Uniform swelling of a whole digit reflects joint and tendon sheath inflammation
Terminal finger joint involvement and nail changes are characteristic
Rheumatoid serology is typically negative in this condition
Conventional agents work for peripheral but not for axial disease
Hidden plaques behind the ears or at the umbilicus are easily missed
explanation.pearls: Nail involvement is present in about 80 per cent of people with this arthritis compared with roughly 40 per cent of those with skin psoriasis alone, so pitting and onycholysis in a patient with joint pain should raise the diagnosis even before the plaques are found.

subtopic_detail: Large unilateral exudative pleural effusion in a former power station worker that has recurred after drainage with malignant cells not found on two separate fluid samples
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man with three months of increasing breathlessness and a constant dull ache in the right side of his chest that does not change with breathing. He worked as a fitter at a power station through the 1970s and 1980s and has never smoked.

He has lost 5 kg. A right sided effusion was drained four weeks ago, 1.4 litres came off and he felt better for a fortnight, but it has reaccumulated. Fluid sent on that occasion and again last week was exudative by protein and lactate dehydrogenase criteria, with no organisms on culture and no malignant cells on cytology on either sample. His chest computed tomogram shows nodular thickening of the pleura with involvement of the mediastinal surface.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Reduced expansion on the right with stony dullness to the mid zone and absent breath sounds, trachea central, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 48 g/L with serum protein 68 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase 420 units per litre with serum 240 units per litre, fluid cytology negative on two occasions, fluid culture and acid fast bacilli negative, computed tomography showing nodular circumferential pleural thickening including the mediastinal pleura with a moderate effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Refer for local anaesthetic thoracoscopy with direct biopsy of the thickened pleura
options.rationale: Cytology is negative in around half of pleural malignancies of this type, so two negative samples do not exclude it and repeated taps waste months, while nodular mediastinal pleural thickening on imaging demands tissue. Thoracoscopy gives the highest diagnostic yield and allows pleurodesis at the same sitting. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Refer for a third large volume aspiration with cytology on a larger fluid sample
options.rationale: Sending more fluid raises the yield only marginally after two adequate negative samples and the near pair is that both approaches sample the same disease, one from the fluid and one from the pleura itself. A third negative result would leave him where he started weeks later. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Refer for blind percutaneous pleural biopsy using an Abrams needle at the bedside
options.rationale: Blind sampling has a much lower yield for malignant disease because the involvement is patchy, and it retains a place mainly where tuberculous pleuritis is likely and the pleura is diffusely involved. Image guided or direct vision sampling has superseded it. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Refer for bronchoscopy with washings and transbronchial biopsy of the right lower lobe
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is useful when there is a mass or collapse suggesting an endobronchial lesion, and his imaging shows pleural rather than parenchymal disease. It would sample the wrong compartment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Refer for talc pleurodesis through an intercostal catheter without further sampling
options.rationale: Pleurodesis controls recurrent fluid and will be needed, but performing it without a diagnosis removes the effusion that makes further sampling possible and forecloses treatment decisions and compensation claims. Tissue first, then palliation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

explanation.summary: A unilateral exudative effusion with weight loss and non-pleuritic chest wall pain in someone with a history of asbestos exposure should be pursued to a tissue diagnosis, because cytology alone misses a large proportion of pleural malignancy and is particularly insensitive for mesothelial tumours. Australia has among the highest rates of asbestos related disease in the world and the latency from exposure is typically 30 to 40 years, so occupational histories from decades earlier remain relevant, including trades, power generation, shipbuilding, construction and home renovation. Computed tomography features that raise concern are circumferential nodular pleural thickening, thickening greater than 1 cm, involvement of the mediastinal pleural surface and volume loss on the affected side. Thoracoscopy under local anaesthetic combines the highest diagnostic yield with the opportunity to perform pleurodesis, and a confirmed diagnosis matters not only for treatment but for access to Australian statutory compensation schemes.
key_points: Pleural fluid cytology misses around half of mesothelial malignancies
Nodular, mediastinal or over 1 cm pleural thickening indicates malignancy
Latency after asbestos exposure is typically thirty to forty years
Thoracoscopy has the highest yield and allows simultaneous pleurodesis
A tissue diagnosis underpins access to compensation schemes
explanation.pearls: Chest wall pain that is constant and dull rather than pleuritic, in a patient with an effusion, points towards pleural infiltration rather than inflammation, and it is the symptom most often present at the first presentation of asbestos related pleural malignancy.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease
BMJ Best Practice: Malignant pleural mesothelioma

subtopic_detail: New firm persistent unilateral parotid enlargement over three months in a woman with established sicca syndrome, a falling C4 and a new paraprotein
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 57 year old woman with an eight year history of dry eyes and dry mouth, anti Ro antibodies and a previous labial gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic infiltration. She manages with artificial tears and frequent sips of water.

For the past three months her left parotid has been enlarging. It is not painful, it does not fluctuate with meals, and it has not settled with a course of antibiotics from her general practitioner. She has had drenching night sweats twice in the last month and has lost 3 kg. Her complement C4 has fallen from 0.22 to 0.08 g/L over a year and a small monoclonal band has appeared on serum electrophoresis that was not present previously.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Firm non-tender 4 cm left parotid enlargement with no overlying erythema and no facial nerve weakness, right parotid normal, no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable, spleen tip palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, dry buccal mucosa with dental caries
data_table.Investigations: Complement C4 0.08 g/L (0.15-0.45) fallen from 0.22, complement C3 0.94 g/L (0.80-1.80), small immunoglobulin M kappa monoclonal band on serum electrophoresis that was absent a year ago, anti Ro antibody positive, rheumatoid factor positive at high titre, lactate dehydrogenase 310 units per litre (120-250), full blood count with lymphocytes 1.1 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a further course of antibiotics with sialogogues and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Bacterial infection of the gland is painful, tender and erythematous, often with pus expressible from the duct, and it responds to antibiotics within days. Three months of painless firm enlargement that has already failed antibiotics is a different problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start hydroxychloroquine for her underlying disease and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine helps fatigue and arthralgia in this condition but has no effect on glandular swelling of this kind, and the near pair is that treating the autoimmune disease feels responsive while the actual concern goes unassessed for a quarter of a year. Systemic symptoms and a new band demand explanation first. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone at a moderate dose and review the size of the gland in one month
options.rationale: Corticosteroid shrinks lymphoid tissue temporarily and can obscure the histology if biopsy follows, making the tissue diagnosis harder to obtain. It also treats the wrong process if the swelling is neoplastic. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Arrange a repeat labial salivary gland biopsy to reassess the degree of infiltration
options.rationale: Minor gland biopsy is used to establish the original diagnosis and would simply reconfirm what is already known, since it samples a different site from the enlarging gland. Sampling must target the abnormal tissue. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent imaging of the gland with biopsy of the enlarged parotid tissue
options.rationale: Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in this condition, especially with a falling C4, a new monoclonal band, splenomegaly and systemic symptoms, is the recognised presentation of lymphoma arising in the gland, and tissue is required to make that diagnosis. Imaging maps the gland and the biopsy is taken with care for the facial nerve. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

explanation.summary: Primary Sjogren syndrome carries a risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma some 15 to 20 times that of the general population, the highest of any autoimmune rheumatic disease, and the tumour most often arises in the affected salivary tissue as a marginal zone lymphoma. The predictors that should prompt vigilance are persistent or recurrent parotid enlargement, palpable purpura, low complement C4, cryoglobulins, a monoclonal band, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia, and they accumulate over years rather than appearing suddenly. Because the risk is lifelong, these features are checked at annual review rather than only when the patient complains. Ordinary glandular swelling in the condition is usually bilateral, episodic and modest, so a unilateral gland that keeps growing over months is the presentation that changes the diagnosis. Treatment of the underlying dryness remains symptomatic with tear and saliva substitutes, muscarinic agonists and meticulous dental care.
key_points: Lymphoma risk is roughly fifteen to twenty times the background rate
Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement is the classic warning sign
Low C4, cryoglobulins and a monoclonal band are validated predictors
Corticosteroid before biopsy can obscure the histological diagnosis
Annual review should actively look for these predictors
explanation.pearls: A falling complement C4 in this condition is not a marker of disease activity in the way it is in lupus but a predictor of lymphoma, so a C4 that drifts down over successive annual reviews should trigger examination of the glands, nodes and spleen rather than an increase in immunosuppression.

subtopic_detail: Enlarging hands and feet with new snoring, carpal tunnel symptoms and difficult to control diabetes and hypertension in a man in his forties
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old man whose wedding ring had to be cut off last year and who has gone up three shoe sizes in a decade. He has come today about numbness in both hands that wakes him at night.

His wife says he has begun snoring heavily and stops breathing at times. His blood pressure has needed a third agent this year and his glycated haemoglobin has risen from 7.1 to 8.4 per cent despite metformin and good adherence. He has a persistent headache most mornings and has noticed his teeth feel further apart. Photographs from ten years ago show a visibly different face with finer features and a less prominent jaw.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Broad spade like hands with doughy soft tissue, prominent supraorbital ridges and mandible with interdental separation, macroglossia, Tinel sign positive at both wrists, visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea, skin tags over the neck
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 8.4 per cent, fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), calcium and thyroid function within normal limits, prolactin 620 milliunits per litre (less than 500)

lead_in: Which investigation should be performed first?

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level on a morning fasting blood sample
options.rationale: Pulsatile secretion means a random level can be low in someone with the disease and high in someone without it, so it neither confirms nor excludes anything. The near pair matters because both tests interrogate the same axis but only one gives an integrated measure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 against an age matched reference range
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses and a single random level is uninterpretable, whereas insulin like growth factor 1 integrates secretion over days and is the recommended initial screening test, compared against an age matched range because the normal value falls with age. An elevated result then leads to a suppression test and imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure growth hormone during a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test this week
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress during a glucose load is the confirmatory test, performed after an elevated integrated marker rather than as the entry point, and it is cumbersome in a man whose glucose control is already poor. Sequence matters here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: Imaging localises a lesion once excess secretion is proven biochemically, and performed first it will find incidental pituitary lesions in around one in ten people, committing him to surgery for a possibly irrelevant finding. Biochemistry precedes anatomy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography to quantify the severity of his sleep disordered breathing
options.rationale: A sleep study will be needed because obstructive sleep apnoea affects most patients with this condition and contributes to the hypertension, but it characterises a consequence rather than the cause. Treating the apnoea alone leaves the driving process untouched. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Obstructive sleep apnoea)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Obstructive sleep apnoea

explanation.summary: Growth hormone excess in adults develops so gradually that the median delay from first symptom to diagnosis is close to a decade, and patients usually present with a consequence rather than with the appearance, most often carpal tunnel syndrome, sleep apnoea, difficult hypertension, new or worsening diabetes, arthropathy or headache. Serial photographs are among the most useful bedside tools because the facial change is invisible to those who see the person daily. The biochemical sequence is an integrated marker first, then failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 microgram per litre during an oral glucose load, then pituitary imaging, and roughly a third of tumours co-secrete prolactin so a modestly raised prolactin fits rather than contradicts the diagnosis. Treatment is transsphenoidal surgery in the first instance, with somatostatin analogues, dopamine agonists, a growth hormone receptor antagonist and radiotherapy available for residual disease, and the excess mortality is largely reversed when hormone levels are normalised. Colonoscopy is recommended at diagnosis because of the increased incidence of colonic neoplasia.
key_points: Presentation is usually via a complication rather than the appearance itself
Old photographs demonstrate the change better than any examination finding
Insulin like growth factor 1 is the screening test, not random growth hormone
Failure to suppress during a glucose load is the confirmatory test
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because incidental lesions are common
explanation.pearls: A modestly raised prolactin supports rather than argues against the diagnosis, because about a third of these tumours co-secrete prolactin or compress the stalk, and treating the raised prolactin as the primary problem is a well described route to a missed diagnosis.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Obstructive sleep apnoea

subtopic_detail: Palpable purpura on the legs with arthralgia and a mildly abnormal sensory examination in a man with untreated chronic hepatitis C, a low C4 and a positive rheumatoid factor
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 55 year old man with six months of crops of raised purple spots over both shins that come and go, leaving brown staining behind. He also has aching in both wrists and a numb patch over the outer side of the left calf.

He was diagnosed with hepatitis C fifteen years ago after injecting drug use, has never been treated and has not injected for twelve years. He has no ascites, no encephalopathy and no varices on a gastroscopy last year, and his transient elastography reading was in the mild fibrosis range. His creatinine is normal and his urine shows no blood or protein. He takes no regular medication and has had no recent infection or new drug exposure.

data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over both shins with haemosiderin staining, no ulceration or digital infarcts, wrists tender with no synovitis, reduced pinprick sensation over the left lateral calf with normal power and reflexes, no hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis C antibody positive with detectable hepatitis C ribonucleic acid at 1.2 million international units per millilitre, genotype 1a, complement C4 0.04 g/L (0.15-0.45), C3 0.98 g/L (0.80-1.80), rheumatoid factor positive at high titre, cryoglobulins detected, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), urinalysis with no blood or protein, albumin 39 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.9-1.3), platelets 186 x10^9/L (150-450)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start rituximab infusions first and add antiviral therapy once the vasculitis settles
options.rationale: Antibody depleting therapy is added for rapidly progressive kidney involvement, ulcerating skin disease or severe neuropathy, none of which he has, and the near pair matters because both treat the same disease at different levels of severity. His creatinine is normal with a bland urinalysis. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C treatment)

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone alone and taper it over the next several months
options.rationale: Corticosteroid alone suppresses the inflammation while leaving viral replication unchecked and can increase the viral load, so it is used only as short term adjunctive therapy in severe disease. It also carries metabolic and bone costs over months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start pegylated interferon with ribavirin for a twenty four week treatment course
options.rationale: Interferon based regimens were superseded in Australia in 2016 by all oral direct acting agents, which are better tolerated, shorter and far more effective. Interferon can also aggravate the neuropathy. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C treatment)

options.text: Start direct acting antiviral therapy for the underlying chronic viral infection
options.rationale: The vasculitis is driven by immune complexes containing the virus, so clearing the virus resolves the skin, joint and nerve involvement in the majority, and direct acting agents achieve cure rates above 95 per cent with a short oral course. With normal renal function and no organ threatening disease, antiviral therapy alone is the first step. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C treatment)

options.text: Start colchicine with graduated compression stockings and review him in three months
options.rationale: Colchicine and compression are symptomatic measures for cutaneous small vessel inflammation of unclear cause, and they do nothing for the antigen driving the immune complexes. His nerve involvement also indicates disease beyond the skin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Chronic hepatitis C causes disease well beyond the liver, and the best characterised extrahepatic manifestation is a small vessel vasculitis driven by circulating immune complexes containing the virus, rheumatoid factor and immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold. The clinical triad is palpable purpura, arthralgia and fatigue, with peripheral neuropathy and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis marking more extensive disease, and the laboratory signature is a strikingly low complement C4 with a relatively preserved C3 and a positive rheumatoid factor in someone who does not have rheumatoid arthritis. All Australians with chronic hepatitis C are eligible for subsidised direct acting antiviral therapy prescribed in general practice with cure rates above 95 per cent, and eradication resolves the vasculitis in most, though a minority have persistent disease requiring immunosuppression. Severe organ threatening presentations receive rituximab, with or without plasma exchange and corticosteroid, alongside or ahead of antiviral treatment.
key_points: A very low C4 with a preserved C3 is the characteristic complement pattern
Positive rheumatoid factor without rheumatoid arthritis is a useful clue
Purpura, arthralgia and fatigue form the classic triad
Clearing the virus resolves the vasculitis in most patients
Rituximab is reserved for organ threatening kidney, skin or nerve disease
explanation.pearls: Blood for cryoglobulins must reach the laboratory in a prewarmed tube kept at 37 degrees Celsius until the serum is separated, because a sample allowed to cool in transit precipitates the protein into the clot and returns a false negative, which is the commonest reason this diagnosis is missed.
